summary.judgment: The lesson is mathematically strong, contractually exact, visually integrated, and unusually good at turning window folklore into measurable decisions. Validation, the 12-cell numeric fixture, figure/demo registries, predecessor continuity, prerequisite retrieval, the five-exercise tail, and exactly one forward exercise all pass. It is not ready for reviewed status because two 294-555-word content sections lack the rubric-required level-three segmentation and at least two KeyFacts fail the deletion test by restating adjacent body conclusions.

rubric_items.evidence: The first paragraph is the exact declarative course opening: ‘Finite observation convolves the desired spectrum with the window transform, so every leakage repair changes resolution and calibration.’ It states the problem and tradeoff with no question or teaser.

Before the first displayed formula in the retrieval answers, the opening supplies the concrete predecessor failure: ‘a rectangular record let one strong off-grid line cover a much weaker neighbor.’ The first new derivation then starts from the explicit eight-sample complex sinusoid ‘x[n]=e^{j2π(1.5/8)n}, 0≤n<8.’

All five content sections serve the course goal ‘Evaluate analysis windows from main-lobe width, sidelobes, coherent gain, scalloping, and equivalent noise bandwidth’: finite-record convolution establishes leakage; endpoint behavior establishes lobe metrics; the next two sections calibrate tones and noise; the final study forces a choice. No off-goal section was found.

The 4,360-word treatment contains a proved convolution theorem, three definitions, an explicit periodic-window convention, a seven-column metric table, a worked calibration example plus paired body problem, an ENBW derivation, a reproducible 16-phase decision study, five visuals, one live lab, and five mixed closing exercises. It holds its own beside the gold lesson at the intended engineering level.

The analysis-window definition states finite support, the half-open record, the zero extension, canonical rectangle, structurally different periodic Hann, degenerate N=1, an infinite-support near-miss, and an admissibility test. The theorem states finite-transform hypotheses and gives a genuine DTFT multiplication/convolution proof. ENBW states its nonzero coherent-sum boundary and canonical, scale-invariant, degenerate, near-miss, and colored-noise limitations.

The exercises require boundary analysis, refutation, unseen-window derivation and calibration, noise comparison, method selection, unequal-tone strategy choice, and a padding/resolution diagnosis. The body problem for v=[0,1,1,0] is genuinely parallel to the worked four-sample periodic-Hann amplitude audit, while the closing v=[1,2,2,1] item fades support to a new window and adds ENBW/noise classification.

The closed-book gate retrieves the raw DFT sign/scale, the fixed-sample versus padded-grid distinction, off-bin leakage, and the repair classification from DFT Bins, Symmetry, and Scaling. The closing set mixes coherent gain, scalloping, lobe widths, ENBW, exact-DTFT neighborhood evidence, and zero-padding without naming the method in advance.

All six Exercise blocks have Solutions. Each solution shows the setup and inference: the four-case boundary probe distinguishes peak calibration from placement loss and 6 dB crossover; the unseen-window solution derives C_v=6, G_c=1.5, B_e=10/9, calibrated tone and noise power; the forward solution holds the aperture and continuous transform fixed. No trick or answer-only item appears.

Mechanical item count: 0. The unseen-window exercise includes arithmetic but also requires a noise comparison and method diagnosis; the other four closing items are boundary reasoning, false-claim refutation, strategy selection, and a conceptual padding experiment. None is merely substitution into a displayed formula.

The set carries all four target forms: degenerate/boundary probes (‘equal frequency’ and half-bin placement), a plausible false claim (‘Hann and Hamming are alternative spellings’), a transfer derivation for unseen v=[1,2,2,1], and research-shaped window choices with explicit overturning checks.

Exactly one closing exercise reaches forward: the N=64 periodic-Hann comparison of L=64 and L=1024 asks which quantities change and which physical resolution claims do not. Its solution alone contains `<Ref lesson="peak-estimation-and-zero-padding">` and states that the next lesson separates interpolation from physical resolution.

The worst offender is the final KeyFact: ‘the same four-term Blackman–Harris choice fails at N=64 and passes at N=128 because observation length moves the fixed physical neighbor relative to its broad main lobe.’ Lines immediately above already state the identical N=64 failure, N=128 pass, 2.75-to-5.5-bin change, and no-universal-winner conclusion. The coherent-gain KeyFact likewise repeats the preceding statement that peak correction does not remove off-bin placement loss or masking. The retrieval Aside passes because it supplies otherwise hidden feedback; the main-lobe/sidelobe KeyFact is a useful synthesis; the ENBW KeyFact at least separates the 1.5 power cost from 0.5 coherent gain.
rubric_items.action: Cut or upgrade the final and coherent-gain KeyFacts; reapply the deletion test to the ENBW KeyFact while editing.

rubric_items.evidence: The two Harris mentions buy checkable distinctions: his 6 dB coherent two-line criterion explains why null-to-null width is not the relevant measure, and his coherent-signal-gain terminology explains G_c versus C_w. No borrowed proof is presented as the lesson author's proof and no source is named for flavour.

A full prose scan found no stale build narration, ‘recreated below’ language, obvious-interface narration, or idiom-for-flavour. Phrases such as ‘The argument uses the DTFT multiplication theorem, not sampling’ and ‘Local leakage is not the headline sidelobe number’ mark mathematical boundaries rather than narrating the apparatus.

Each visual carries a distinct inference: the four-frame sequence exposes the periodic boundary repair; WindowShapeSpectrumPair separates width, peak sidelobe, and far falloff; WindowCalibrationLedger separates coherent sums from squared-weight noise; the masking SVG makes the -1.62 dB failure visible; WindowTradeoffMap shows why two metrics cannot rank every geometry. Every caption states a fact or task, not merely pictured objects.

The prose asks the learner to precommit, falsify narrowest-is-best at rectangular N=128, compare equal-N windows, then raise short Blackman–Harris from N=64 to N=128. WeakToneWindowLab starts alive on the -1.619 dB failure, offers four named presets and explicit targets, hides the audit after manual choices, sweeps 16 deterministic phases, and gives synchronous local-leakage and five-metric feedback. Its threshold-finding/all-phase behavior cannot be replaced by the static one-phase figure.

Paragraph cadence between apparatus blocks is acceptable, but ‘Finite observation creates leakage before an FFT is chosen’ is 555 words with no `###`, and ‘Equivalent noise bandwidth uses squared weights’ is 294 words with no `###`. The other 552-749-word sections are segmented; these two violate the explicit over-about-200-word rule.

rubric_items.evidence: The skeleton reconstructs the argument without folds: ‘Finite observation creates leakage before an FFT is chosen’ → ‘Endpoint behavior exchanges a narrow main lobe for lower sidelobes’ → ‘Coherent gain and scalloping calibrate deterministic tones’ → ‘Equivalent noise bandwidth uses squared weights’ → ‘A weak neighbor turns the metrics into a decision.’ Captions add boundary repair, lobe redistribution, two calibration paths, the masking failure, and the no-universal-winner conclusion.

Italics mark first-use or convention terms (‘analysis window,’ ‘periodic,’ ‘original’); bold marks metric names, misconception labels, and run-in solution labels. Four em dashes over 4,360 words are below the density limit, and literal technical identifiers are not styled as tonal emphasis.

The prose is dry, precise, and declarative throughout. A complete scan found zero rhetorical questions, teasers, invented scenes, or chatty asides. Terms such as coherent gain, scalloping loss, ENBW, local leakage, periodic coefficients, and original-bin coordinates are defined at first use.

All four references are real, relevant, and chapter-precise: Harris 1978 names §§III–IV, Table I, and §VI for leakage/window metrics/resolution; Smith names Chapter 3 and §§5.4–5.5 for analysis windows and shifted kernels; Oppenheim–Schafer–Buck names Chapter 10 §§10.1–10.2 for finite-data Fourier analysis; MIT 6.341 names Lecture 17 pp.1–3 and Problem Set 9 problems 9.1–9.5. The Stanford and MIT links resolve, IEEE document 1455106 identifies Harris's paper, and MIT's official index lists lec17.pdf and ps9.pdf.

The paragraph after the opening explicitly inherits the predecessor's strong-off-grid/weak-neighbor failure, names the DFT finite-record sampling prerequisite, and states the contribution: ‘five measurements’ tested against ‘one phase-robust weak-tone claim.’ This matches the spine step ‘Finite records trade leakage against resolution.’

Sampled seams connect cleanly: endpoint behavior opens from ‘The convolution model says every tone inherits W,’ coherent calibration opens by reversing the normalized-lobe plot's hidden attenuation, ENBW opens by contrasting deterministic coherent sums with independent-noise squared sums, and the decision section opens by turning the five separate metrics into one signal claim.

The last content paragraph establishes that main lobe/sidelobes set interference while coherent gain/scalloping/ENBW calibrate claims, then names the unresolved task: locating an isolated tone between displayed coordinates without confusing denser sampling with longer observation. Its Ref to Peak Estimation and Zero-Padding Limits matches the next course spine step.

All five content headings are claims rather than topics: finite observation creates leakage; endpoint behavior exchanges width for sidelobes; coherent gain/scalloping calibrate tones; ENBW uses squared weights; a weak neighbor turns metrics into a decision.

Cover tests pass on the endpoint and weak-neighbor sections. Removing their seam and last sentences still leaves the coefficient-convention warning, metric table, smoothness/peak distinction, exact two-tone contract, all-phase rule, frozen pass/fail table, and the two falsified scalar heuristics; the bearing remains visible and neither body is an inventory.

Phone-Channel DTMF Receiver closes with the exact N=205 rectangular result: normalized leakage 0.212225 at d=1.5, -13.4641 dB, 26.5359 dB above the weak line, plus the statement that padding does not remove it. This lesson opens by naming that unresolved masking curve and immediately supplies the promised five window measurements. The join requires no inference from the reader.

No secondary survey narrates the lesson. Harris is named only where provenance is content—the origin of coherent-signal-gain terminology and the particular 6 dB two-line resolution criterion—and the detailed literature pointers remain in References.
No geography, dated human event, or place-dense paragraph occurs in this engineering lesson.

Named terms are paced and glossed on arrival. The window-convention paragraph introduces rectangular, Hann, Hamming, and one coefficient-fixed four-term Blackman–Harris family together because their formulas are the object of one comparison; later paragraphs introduce no comparable proper-name pileup.

The opening recalls both earlier lessons with explicit Refs and reminder clauses: the predecessor's masked weak line and the prerequisite's fact that the DFT samples the continuous transform of one finite record. The retrieval Aside gives full feedback on sign/scale, padding, leakage, and physical repairs.

Sampled numeric sentences retain frames: 1.5 cycles across an eight-sample aperture; one current-record bin equals 2π/N radians/sample; -40 dB is tied to amplitude 0.01; the fixed 5.5-bin separation is defined against N0=128; the local grid is [25.5,26.5] in 1/64 original-bin steps; every margin states dB and its ≥3.000 dB consequence.

Keeper numbers live in the seven-column metric table, WindowShapeSpectrumPair, WindowCalibrationLedger, the masking SVG, the frozen decision table, and the interactive readouts. Prose uses only load-bearing values needed to define conventions, calibrations, or the reproducible contract.
No human event is rendered as a data row.

Deletion-tested details are load-bearing: N versus N-1 fixes periodic/symmetric metrics; the N=4 Hann weights feed the paired exercise and calibration figure; 6 dB width drives the first boundary exercise; N0=128 fixes the demo coordinate system; 16 phases and the 65-point grid make the verdict reproducible; -1.62/12.55/59.16 dB outcomes drive the guided targets.
The lesson uses original analytic SVGs and React-rendered diagrams only; there is no sourced raster or text scan.

Two genuine window-selection misconceptions are explicitly refuted with counterevidence and replacements: ‘narrowest is best’ fails because rectangular sidelobes mask the weak neighbor, while ‘lowest sidelobe is best’ fails for short Blackman–Harris because the fixed pair lies in its broad central neighborhood. The Hann/Hamming spelling misconception is rejected and retrieved in a closing exercise.

Importance is carried by stable Definition, Theorem, Example, Task, KeyFact, Figure, Demo, and Exercise roles plus a separate optional retrieval Aside. A scan found no ‘obviously,’ ‘crucially,’ ‘very important,’ or equivalent intensifier standing in for structure.
